title: Causality can systematically address the monsters under the bench(marks)
claim: A small causal graph shows a shared confounder driving both the input and the outcome, so a direct input-output link can mislead.
layout: Single panel, triangle of three nodes, top-to-bottom and left-to-right arrows
description: A hand-drawn, sketchy causal diagram with three scribbled ellipses on a white background. A light-blue node labeled 'Problem' sits at top center. A peach node labeled 'Prompt' sits at lower left. A teal node labeled 'Response' sits at lower right. Arrows run from Problem down-left to Prompt and down-right to Response. A third arrow runs horizontally from Prompt to Response. The result is a triangle in which Problem is a common cause of Prompt and Response, and Prompt also affects Response directly. Each node has a pastel fill with a thick black wobbly outline. The eye goes first to the large top node, then follows the arrows. There is no math notation and no legend. The image does not show the two data panels the caption describes (a ACL-paper trend plot and a term-clustering dendrogram), so the crop appears to be a different figure.
caption: (a) Percentage of ACL Anthology papers mentioning "reasoning", "reasoner", or "reasoners" in their titles or abstracts, and the subset also mentioning "causal" or "causality", 2016--2026. Error bars show 95% Wilson binomial reference intervals under an independent-paper model. (b) Unconstrained complete-linkage clustering of term groups across the 10,628 reasoning papers in the same period, using Euclidean distances between absolute-correlation profiles. Green highlights the smallest subtree containing the five causal term groups, which also includes "spurious"; coloring does not constrain clustering. Parenthetical counts give the number of papers mentioning each term group. Data were retrieved from the ACL Anthology on November 5, 2026.
abstract: Effective and reliable evaluation is essential for advancing empirical machine learning. However, the increasing accessibility of generalist models and the progress towards ever more complex, high-level tasks make systematic evaluation more challenging. Benchmarks are plagued by various biases, artifacts, or leakage, while models may behave unreliably due to poorly explored failure modes. Haphazard treatments and inconsistent formulations of such "monsters" leads to a duplication of efforts, a lack of trust in results, and unsupported inferences. In this position paper, we argue causality offers an ideal framework to systematically address these challenges. By making causal assumptions in an approach explicit, we can faithfully model phenomena, formulate testable hypotheses with explanatory power, and leverage principled tools for analysis. To make the design of conceptual causal models more accessible, we identify several useful Common Abstract Topologies (CATs) in causal graphs which help gain insight into the reasoning abilities in large language models. Through a series of case studies, we demonstrate how the precise yet pragmatic language of causality clarifies the strengths and limitations of a method and inspires new approaches for systematic progress.
